fact_sheet.business_description: The Coca-Cola Company sells branded beverage concentrates through a worldwide bottling and distribution system [D01]. The company relies on a flagship product with high repeat consumer demand and global recognition [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Branded beverage concentrates sold to bottlers and retailers who manage final production and access [D01, D06]. Customers purchase based on brand identity, with repeat demand supported by advertising and quality [D01, D06].
economics: 1987 operating margin was 17.3% [D02]. Return on average equity from continuing operations was 27.2% in 1987 [D02]. Concentrate model requires less capital than bottling, though advertising and route-to-market access require resources [D01, D06].
earnings_record: Net income: $559m (1983), $629m (1984), $722m (1985), $934m (1986), $916m (1987) [D02]. 1987 reported net income decline of 1.9% attributed to nonoperating items, while EPS rose 0.4% [D03].
competitive_position: Global soft-drink share of more than 44% (excluding USSR/China) [D06]. Market reach exceeds 155 countries with 524m+ daily servings [D06].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Total debt of $2,702m as of 1987 year-end [D02]. FY1987 cash and marketable securities were $1,468m [D02]. Simple net debt of $1,234m [D02].
management_and_capital_allocation: CEO Roberto Goizueta (since 1981) and Don Keough focus on the beverage franchise and financial discipline [D01]. Buybacks/dividends record includes $1.12 cash dividend in 1987 [D02].
price_and_valuation: 1987 year-end closing price $38.13 [D04]. P/E 15.69x and P/B 4.40x at 1987 year-end [D04]. Earnings yield 6.37% (1987) vs 8.87% ten-year Treasury yield (Sept 30, 1988) [D04].
what_the_market_is_worried_about: Franchise fully valued, potential disappointment in international growth, dilution from capital-heavy bottling/unrelated activities, and competitive pressure from rivals [D05].
recent_events: Second-quarter 1988 net income up 13.8% [D03]. July 1988 report cited European/Pacific sales and dollar decline as growth factors [D03].
berkshire_context: Major existing interests include Capital Cities/ABC, GEICO, and Washington Post [D08]. Berkshire holdings information as of 1986 year-end is stale [D08].
document_conflicts: 1986 continuing-income ROE cited as 28.8% in D02, noting 23.8% in a secondary transcription is erroneous.
missing_data: Current September 30, 1988 market quotation, current trailing earnings multiple, and precise maintenance capex reconciliation for owner earnings calculation [D02, D04].

understandable.evidence: The company maintains a consistent flagship product with high repeat consumer demand and global recognition [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: The company holds a global market share exceeding 44% with strong brand identity across 155 countries [D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Net income showed growth from $559m in 1983 to $916m in 1987 despite temporary fluctuations [D02, D03].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: Return on average equity reached 27.2% in 1987 with a manageable net debt position of $1,234m against significant cash reserves [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The concentrate business model is inherently less capital-intensive than bottling, allowing for efficient growth [D01].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Management focuses on the beverage franchise and financial discipline, evidenced by consistent dividends and share buybacks [D01, D02].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: The company's scale and earnings power are significant enough to provide meaningful impact for Berkshire [D02, D06].

price_screen.evidence: The 6.37% earnings yield is significantly below the 10% threshold and lower than the 8.87% ten-year Treasury yield [D04].

conflicts_resolved: 1986 ROE conflict: relied on 28.8% as the corrected figure per document [D02].
gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a world-class consumer franchise with an immense moat, high returns on capital, and exceptional brand loyalty.

gate2.why_available: The market currently focuses on short-term competitive pressures and the potential for dilution from bottling acquisitions, which leads them to ignore the durable, compounding nature of the global concentrate franchise [D05]. We disagree, as the brand's immense moat and pricing power will allow per-share earnings to grow significantly over time regardless of temporary market noise [D01, D06]. The value will materialize as the company continues its record of efficient capital allocation and high returns on equity [D02].
evidence: Global soft-drink share exceeding 44% with reach in 155 countries [D06].
Return on average equity consistently high, reaching 27.2% in 1987 [D02].
Management focuses on the core beverage franchise and disciplined capital allocation [D01].
Second-quarter 1988 net income growth of 13.8% demonstrating continued momentum [D03].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market views the franchise as fully valued and fears that international growth potential is limited or that diversification into bottling will impair returns [D05].
what_must_be_true: The brand remains the dominant global choice for soft drinks.
Management continues to prioritize the concentrate business over dilutive, capital-intensive diversifications.
The inherent pricing power remains intact to offset any inflationary pressures.
The competitive landscape does not meaningfully erode the long-term volume of daily servings.

gate3.owner_earnings_per_share: Not explicitly provided in pack; estimated using 1987 EPS of $2.43 [D04] adjusted for low maintenance capex requirements inherent in the concentrate model [D01]

intrinsic_value_range.low: Conservative estimate based on 12-15x owner earnings
intrinsic_value_range.high: Optimistic estimate based on 20x+ owner earnings reflecting long-term compounding
key_assumptions: Maintenance capex remains minimal relative to concentrate model [D01]

gate3.price_vs_value: Price appears fair relative to the durable compounding potential; margin of safety exists if long-term volume growth is sustained [D05]
gate3.alternatives: Long-term bonds yield 8.87% [D04]. Coca-Cola offers superior potential for real growth in earnings and dividends compared to fixed income [D02].
gate3.downside_case: Permanent loss is unlikely due to the global dominance of the brand [D06] and the franchise's pricing power; downside is limited to multiple contraction if growth expectations are not met [D05].
flagged_assumptions: Maintenance capex is assumed to be nominal due to the concentrate business model [D01]
Current 1988 earnings are projected based on 13.8% H1 growth [D03]

gate4.role_description: We are a permanent passive holder. We look for wonderful businesses at fair prices to own for the long term, allowing the underlying economics and capital allocation to compound our value [D01, D06].
value_realisation_path: Disciplined capital allocation by management through dividends and buybacks [D01, D02]
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: Post-1980, we focus on identifying consumer franchises with durable competitive advantages and holding them indefinitely; Coca-Cola's global brand moat and concentrate business model make it a premier candidate for a permanent position [D01, D06].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of global brand preference to competitors.
Management shifts strategy away from the high-margin concentrate model into capital-intensive, low-return bottling or unrelated diversifications.
Persistent decline in volume of daily servings due to a changing regulatory or health environment.
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must maintain sufficient cash reserves to protect against insurance liabilities and ensure liquidity for opportunistic purchases [D02].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Comparison to existing consumer franchise holdings like Capital Cities/ABC and GEICO, and the superior real growth potential of Coca-Cola versus the 8.87% yield of ten-year Treasury bonds [D04, D08].
gate5.decider_reason: The position is a core consumer franchise with an immense moat and durable economics that fits squarely within my circle of competence and capacity for major capital allocation.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The primary risk is a potential multiple contraction if market growth expectations for the concentrate business are not met, though the underlying business economics remain exceptionally durable.

valuation.owner_earnings: Estimated using $2.43 EPS adjusted for low maintenance capex [D04, D01].
valuation.intrinsic_value_range: Conservative at 12-15x owner earnings, optimistic at 20x+ due to compounding [D03].
valuation.downside_case: Multiple contraction, though permanent loss is highly unlikely given brand dominance [D05, D06].

drivers.driver: The company possesses an unparalleled global consumer franchise with over 44% market share and immense pricing power [D06].
The concentrate-based business model is exceptionally capital-efficient, allowing for high returns on equity [D01, D02].
Management, led by Roberto Goizueta, acts like owners by focusing on the beverage franchise and disciplined capital allocation [D01].
The market's obsession with short-term competitive noise ignores the durable, long-term compounding nature of the global brand [D05].
Per-share earnings growth of 15% demonstrates the compounding potential that justifies a fair entry price today [D03].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of global brand preference to competitors.
Management shifts strategy away from the high-margin concentrate model into capital-intensive, low-return bottling or unrelated diversifications.
Persistent decline in volume of daily servings due to a changing regulatory or health environment.
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A fundamental erosion of the brand's global preference or a shift toward dilutive, capital-intensive strategies that compromise the concentrate model's economics.
final.memo:
We have long admired The Coca-Cola Company, a business whose product is consumed over 500 million times daily across 155 countries [D06]. It is a simple business that we understand: the company sells branded concentrates to a global bottling system, relying on deep consumer loyalty built over decades [D01].

This is a premier franchise, evidenced by a global market share exceeding 44% and an ability to command pricing that stays ahead of inflation [D06]. The economics are wonderful; because the concentrate model requires minimal capital, the company consistently generates returns on equity exceeding 27% [D01, D02].

Roberto Goizueta and Don Keough have run the business with admirable discipline and an owner-oriented mindset [D01]. They have focused on the core beverage franchise while consistently returning cash to shareholders through dividends and buybacks [D02].

The market currently appears fixated on short-term competitive pressures and the potential impact of bottling investments [D05]. We believe these worries miss the forest for the trees; the strength of the brand and its compounding ability are far more significant than the noise of any single quarter [D05].

While the initial earnings yield is lower than that of long-term bonds, the growth prospects for a world-class franchise like Coke are vastly superior [D04]. We expect this business to compound our value indefinitely [D01].

We intend to build this into a significant position, perhaps 20% of our equity portfolio, as we view it as a cornerstone asset [D05]. We would only rethink our commitment if the global preference for the brand were to permanently decline or if management strayed from the high-margin concentrate business [D01, D06].
